paper_title: Change the Base, Change the Game: Rethinking Pan-sharpening

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Many pan-sharpening (PS) networks reconstruct high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) images by adding learned residuals to 4$\times$-interpolated low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) inputs, incorporating panchromatic (PAN) detail only through these residual corrections. This raises a simple question: Why start with a blurry base when sharp spatial detail is already available? We propose PanBase, a sharper multispectral starting point designed for more effective residual learning. Guided by physical sensor characteristics, PanBase combines PAN spatial detail with LRMS spectral information while enforcing consistency with the LRMS observations under sensor-specific blur. We construct this base without neural network training, estimating only nine coefficients per spectral band through closed-form calibration. Our PanBase can be easily integrated into existing backbones with a global residual skip through two simple changes: (i) replacing the skip base with PanBase and (ii) concatenating it as an additional input. Using each backbone's original training recipe and matched training budgets, PanBase improves most reduced- and full-resolution metrics on WorldView-3, QuickBird, and GaoFen-2, while achieving 4.4$\times$ faster training convergence on average. In zero-shot evaluation on WorldView-2, standalone PanBase achieves competitive reconstruction without target-sensor fitting or neural refinement.

In zero-shot evaluation on WorldView2, standalone PanBase achieves competitive reconstruction without target-sensor fitting or neural refinement. 1. Introduction Residual learning is widely used in image restoration, including super-resolution [19], denoising [46], and deblurring [6]. In this approach, global skip connection carries an initial estimate, or base, derived from the available observations, such as low-resolution, noisy, or blurred images. The network adds its predicted residual to this base to reconstruct the target. base that captures more of the target structure leaves less for the network to recover, which can accelerate convergence and improve reconstruction quality. Pan-sharpening (PS) offers natural opportunity to build more informative base because it reconstructs highresolution multispectral (HRMS) image from two complementary observations: panchromatic (PAN) image with fine spatial detail and low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) image with band-specific spectral information. (i) Starting from PAN, PS resembles colorization: PAN provides the spatial structure, and LRMS guides the recovery of the spectral bands. (ii) Starting from LRMS, PS resembles 4 super-resolution: LRMS provides the spectral information, and PAN guides the recovery of fine spatial detail. In either view, one observation provides the starting point and the other guides the recovery of what is missing. This raises natural question: Why not build better base from both observations before training the residual network? Recent PS methods have improved residual prediction through adaptive convolutions [11, 37], modality-aware attention [10], state-space models [28], and diffusion [20]. Yet many residual networks still use interpolated LRMS as the base in their global skip connection [45]. Although the residual branch receives PAN, the base does not directly incorporate its fine spatial detail. This leaves an opportunity to improve the starting point itself using detail that is already available in PAN. In this paper, we propose PanBase, sharper multispectral base constructed from PAN and LRMS before backbone training. Guided by the sensors physical characteristics, PanBase incorporates spatial detail from PAN while ensuring that the resulting base reproduces the observed LRMS after sensor-specific blur and downsampling. Constructing the base requires no neural network training: closed-form ridge regression [16] calibrates just nine coefficients per spectral band, giving 36 and 72 coefficients for fourand eight-band images, respectively. Fig. 1 shows that PanBase provides sharper starting point even before neural refinement. We integrate PanBase with only two changes: (i) replacing interpolated LRMS with PanBase in the global skip and (ii) concatenating PanBase with the original inputs. This design is compatible with diverse backbones that use global image-space residual connection, including convolution-, attention-, state-space-, and diffusion-based models. On PanCollection datasets, adding PanBase improves most reduced-resolution (RR) and full-resolution (FR) metrics on WorldView-3, QuickBird, and GaoFen-2 under matched training budgets. Across all four sensors, including WorldView-2, it improves RR PSNR in 39 of 40 matched comparisons, with gains of up to 6.93 dB. PanBase alone outperforms all compared classical methods in all metrics across the four sensors. On unseen WorldView-2, PanBase reuses the 72 coefficients calibrated on WorldView-3 and achieves 30.12 dB PSNR, surpassing all original backbones in the main comparison without target-sensor fitting or neural refinement. PanBase also accelerates training convergence by factor of 4.4 on average, while keeping the cost of base construction modest. For four-band data, the one-time calibration takes 88 to load 6,000 training patches and accumulate calibration statistics, followed by 16 ms for the coefficient solves. Once the coefficients and sensor operators are in place, constructing four-band 256256 base takes 0.19 on CPU. Our contributions are threefold: We rethink residual pan-sharpening by changing its starting point: PanBase incorporates the sharp spatial detail already available in PAN into the multispectral base before residual learning, while preserving consistency with the observed LRMS. We calibrate just nine coefficients per spectral band in closed form and integrate PanBase into existing residual backbones by replacing the global skip base and concatenating PanBase with the original inputs. Across ten backbones and four sensors, matched comparisons show RR PSNR gains of up to 6.93 dB and faster training, while standalone PanBase transfers to an unseen sensor without recalibration. 2. sections.title: Traditional PS methods
sections.content: Traditional methods. include component substitution (CS), multiresolution analysis (MRA), and variational optimization (VO) [32, 36]. CS transfers spatial structure by substituting an MS-derived intensity component with PAN [3, 7, 23, 31]. MRA extracts PAN detail through multiscale decomposition and injects it into upsampled MS using band-dependent gains [2, 5, 25, 29, 34]. VO reconstructs HRMS by optimizing 2 Figure 2. Projection enforces LRMS consistency under the sensor model. (b) The base replaces the global skip and is concatenated with the backbone inputs; added input-channel weights are zero-initialized. observation fidelity together with spatial or spectral priors [26, 27, 33, 41]. While these methods directly reconstruct HRMS, PanBase uses the sensors physical imaging model to combine PAN spatial detail with LRMS spectral information into an observation-consistent starting point for residual learning. Learning-based methods. Early CNN-based methods, such as PanNet, introduced residual learning for spatial spectral reconstruction [45]. Subsequent designs improve feature aggregation through adaptive convolutions in LAGConv [18] and encourage complementary PAN MS representations through mutual information learning in MutInf [47]. HFIN extends fusion to hierarchical spatialfrequency representations [30], while PAN-Crafter addresses PANMS misalignment through modality-aware attention [10]. Recent methods further explore two-step spatialspectral enhancement in TS-Pan [21] and efficient binary reconstruction in BNNPan [17]. State-space models also support long-range feature interaction [28]. Beyond architectural advances, MDCUN embeds degradation models into deep unfolding [43], while PINO incorporates sensor imaging physics into learned fusion [22]. PanFlowNet further explores probabilistic reconstruction through conditional normalizing flows [44]. Diffusion-based methods extend generative reconstruction through text conditioning [42], uncertainty-aware distillation [20], and few-step sampling [12]. PanBase complements these approaches with sharper, observation-consistent base constructed in closed form and can be integrated into any backbone with global image-space residual connection. 2.2. Residual Learning for Image Restoration Residual learning preserves an initial estimate and predicts its correction, as in super-resolution [19], denoising [46], and deblurring [6]. The initial estimate defines the residual target and determines which structures remain for the network to recover. In PS, residual networks commonly use upsampled LRMS as the base, introducing PAN spatial detail through the learned correction. PanNet learns spatial corrections in the high-pass domain while preserving spectral information through an upsampled-MS skip [45]. DiCNN directly models the injected MS detail [14], while CS-Net, MRA-Net, and FusionNet connect classical injection formulations with learned nonlinear detail prediction [8]. Related efforts also improve initial estimates through PAN-guided learned upsampling in PGCU [48] or use frozen network-generated spectral base for residual diffusion [40]. PanBase instead constructs the residual reference through closed-form calibration with explicit LRMS consistency, without requiring learned upsampler or preenhancement network. 3.
